captures.transcript:
I opened my mouth.

Closed it.

I hated that he was already getting better at this.

“Years.”

The eye narrowed.

“There were little things early. People saying something differently. A shop closing on the wrong month. Weather. I ignored most of it because people remember weather badly and shops close whenever they feel like failing.”

The larger things came later.

Years later.

That sounded bad when I said it out loud.

“Strongest is close enough for taverns and wrong enough for everything else. One can destroy a crawler nest alone. Another can't, but can walk through pressure that kills the first one. One is better in a city. One is better where there isn't one. Put them all in a field and somebody will write a ranking. Put them in six different disasters and you get six different answers.”

I had been one of them for eleven years officially.

captures.transcript:
“There are no redbacks north of Vey. If there was one, tell me what was beneath the third dorsal plate.”

I stared at him.

Of course that was his question.

“Meat.”

His eye closed.

I felt judged by an eyelid.

“Black tissue. Stringy. Smelled like burnt hair when I cut it.”

The eye opened.

I could see the thing again as I talked.

Not the whole fight.

Memory rarely returned politely.

A patch of wet red hide.

My left boot slipping between plates.

The smell.

A sword hilt slick in my hand.

captures.transcript:
The pupil tightened again.

I had managed to surprise a dragon twice in one morning.

It was not improving my odds of leaving.

“How she got trapped is a long story.”

His chin settled onto the stone.

Not bored this time.

Comfortable.

That was worse.

He was becoming pleased with the existence of long stories.

“In that history she told me your name. She also told me how to cross the mountain.”

Ithar's eye moved to my coat.

The sulfur residue.

The clean boots.

captures.transcript:
“You know my name. I know the paths by which that name moved in this world. You are absent from all of them.

“You offer another history as the missing path. That is not proof. It is better than prophecy and worse than evidence. But it is now a claim with structure.”

I looked at him.

That was the least satisfying way anyone had ever called me interesting.

Still.

Structure was better than being eaten.

Probably.

“So you believe I remember another life.”

Something low moved in his throat.

captures.transcript:
It was not really a seat.

It was a part of the cave that happened to be roughly the right height and only moderately covered in old coins.

My left leg preferred sitting to standing.

The rest of me had not yet decided whether sitting in a dragon's home counted as progress.

“The Line is failing now. That part has a clock. You still haven't agreed to help, so I should probably keep saying it.”

Ithar's claw moved through the gold again.

The sound was becoming background noise.

Deeper into it.

“If the Line were repaired now, what would you do next? Do not give me a direction and call it home. Tell me what home means, and what you intend to do there after the emergency you have used to explain your arrival is gone.”

I looked at him.

“That is several questions pretending to be one.”

His nostril moved.

Fine.

I picked at a split in the leather over my right palm.

The glove was new compared to most of me.

Three months.

Good stitching.

Bad fit around the fingers.

captures.transcript:
The cave suddenly felt warmer.

“Don't.”

His eye remained on me.

I waited.

He waited longer.

I hated him a little.

The claw dragged a shallow line through the gold.

Coins rolled into it and vanished.

He wanted the end of the first life.

I could feel the question coming without hearing it spoken.

“No.”

The pupil shifted.

“We're not doing this. We're discussing the Line.”

As far as Ithar was concerned, we had finished discussing the Line when he refused to promise anything.

captures.transcript:
I laughed when his expression failed to change.

“You're serious.”

Stone ground against stone as Ithar shifted his foreleg beneath him.

Gold slid for several seconds.

Something metal fell deeper in the mound and kept falling long enough that I wondered how far down the hoard went.

When the sound finally stopped, the dragon took the floor again.

“I do not require eighty years in sequence.

captures.transcript:
That might have been the first practical offer he had made me.

Not save the kingdom.

Not repair the Line.

Food directions.

It was a start.

“You understand I have to shit.”

His nostril opened.

“You are welcome to do that outside.”

I laughed.

Ithar did not.

Maybe that was a joke.

I was beginning to think the problem was not that dragons lacked humor.

The problem was that this one did not care whether I noticed.

I finally unbuckled my pack.
